matches.claim: In the example, the virtual machine has a single 40GB virtual hard disk file (vmdk) that is to be increased to 50GB.

matches.claim: Increasing a virtual machine's disk size takes two steps: first increasing the VMDK file size in the VM settings on vCenter/ESXi, then extending the disk partition in the guest OS.
matches.quote: The process of increasing a virtual machine’s disk size takes two steps: - First, you need to increase the VMDK file size in the VM settings on vCenter/ESXi; - Then extend the disk partition in the guest OS

matches.claim: To increase a virtual disk's size in VirtualBox via the Virtual Media Manager, the user selects the dynamic virtual disk file (VDI file) whose storage size should be increased.
matches.quote: Now locate and select the dynamic virtual disk file (VDI file), that you want to increase it's storage size.

matches.claim: For a virtual machine with a FIXED disk, the disk size can only be increased by cloning and converting the FIXED disk to a DYNAMIC disk and then increasing the new dynamic disk's storage space.
matches.quote: If you have setup a virtual machine with a FIXED disk, the only way to increase the disk's size is to first clone and convert – at the same time – the FIXED disk to DYNAMIC and after to increase the storage space on the new created DYNAMIC disk (VDI file), as instructed in Part-1 above.

matches.claim: In the Virtual Media Manager, the storage size of a virtual disk is adjusted with the "Size" slider and saved by clicking Apply.
matches.quote: Use the "Size" slider to adjust the storage size and then click Apply , to save the change.

matches.claim: A dynamic virtual disk's size in VirtualBox can be increased from the command prompt.
matches.quote: The second method to increase the size of a Dynamic virtual disk, in VirtualBox is by using command prompt.

matches.claim: The virtual machine must be shut down before its virtual disk size is increased via command prompt.
matches.quote: Shutdown the Virtual Machine whose virtual disk size you want to increase.

matches.claim: In the VMware VM settings window, the Expand button next to “Expand disk capacity” is clicked on the Hard Disk right panel to expand the disk.
matches.quote: On the right panel, click on the “ Expand ” button next to “Expand disk capacity”.

matches.claim: In the example given, a VMware virtual disk originally of 30GB is expanded by 10GB to a total new drive capacity of 40GB.
matches.quote: For example, I want to expand the disk by 10GB, so I replaced 30 with 40. That way, the total new drive capacity will be 40GB.

matches.claim: The article describes how to resize a virtual machine disk in VMware ESXi and then extend the partition in a Windows or Ubuntu guest OS without stopping or rebooting the virtual machine.
matches.quote: This article describes how to resize a virtual machine disk in VMware ESXi and then extend the partition in Windows or Ubuntu guest OS without stopping or rebooting the virtual machine.

matches.claim: A VMware virtual machine disk cannot be increased if the VM has snapshots, and all snapshots must be removed first.
matches.quote: You cannot increase the disk if the VM has snapshots. All snapshots must be removed;

matches.claim: The error message "Resizing to new size is not yet supported" appears when trying to increase the size of a Fixed disk, because VirtualBox does not allow resizing a Fixed Virtual Disk via its GUI or command prompt.
matches.quote: Note: If you receive the error message "Resizing to new size is not yet supported", read the instructions on Part-2 , because this error appears when you try to increase the size on a Fixed disk, and VirtualBox does not allow to resize a Fixed Virtual Disk, using its GUI interface or via command prompt.

matches.claim: The expand disk window in VMware asks for the total new drive capacity to be entered.
matches.quote: In this window, type in the total new drive capacity of your choice.

matches.claim: After expanding a VMware virtual disk, a new partition must be created or the existing partition extended manually from within the guest operating system.
matches.quote: So, you have to manually create a new partition or extend the existing partition from the guest operating system.

matches.claim: The VMFS datastore must have enough free space to accommodate the disk increase.
matches.quote: Make sure that your VMFS datastore has enough free space.

matches.claim: After a VMware virtual disk is increased in size, the guest operating system does not recognize the extra space, which appears as Unallocated.
matches.quote: Do keep in mind that though you’ve increased the disk size in VMware, the guest operating system doesn’t know it because the extended storage will be listed as Unallocated.

matches.claim: Only virtual disks connected via a virtual SCSI or NVMe controller can be expanded online; disks on an IDE controller require the VM to be shut down first.
matches.quote: Only disks connected via virtual SCSI or NVMe controller can be expanded online (if the virtual disk is connected via IDE controller, the virtual machine must be shut down first);

matches.claim: Online extension of virtual machine disks is only possible if VMware Tools is installed in the guest operating system.

matches.claim: In a Windows guest, the Disk Management tool can be used to create or extend a partition after the VMware disk is increased.
matches.quote: For instance, if you’ve installed Windows in the virtual machine, you can open the Disk Management tool to create or extend partition.

matches.claim: Other risk factors, called co-factors, act along with HPV to increase the risk for cervical cancer.

matches.claim: Infection with HPV, sexual activity, smoking, giving birth many times, infection with HIV, history of sexually transmitted infections, oral contraceptives, and diethylstilbestrol (DES) can increase the risk for cervical cancer.
matches.quote: The following can increase your risk for cervical cancer: Infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) Sexual activity Smoking Giving birth many times Infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) History of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) Oral contraceptives Diethylstilbestrol (DES)

matches.claim: People without any of the listed risk factors rarely develop cervical cancer.

matches.claim: A risk factor increases your chance of getting a disease such as cancer.

matches.claim: Key risk factors for breast cancer include genetics (family history), certain hormonal exposures, obesity, lack of physical activity, and alcohol consumption.
matches.quote: Key risk factors include genetics (family history), certain hormonal exposures (early menstruation, late menopause, never having children or having first child late), obesity, lack of physical activity, and alcohol consumption.

matches.claim: Having many sexual partners is linked with a higher risk of cervical cancer, and a person can have HPV even with only one sexual partner.
matches.quote: For this reason, having many sexual partners is linked with a higher risk of cervical cancer. But you can have HPV even when you’ve had only one sexual partner.

matches.claim: Most cases of cervical cancer occur in women younger than 50 years of age.
matches.quote: Most cases of cervical cancer occur in women younger than 50 years of age.

matches.claim: Smoking is a risk factor for many cancers.
